summary: An April 1st humor RFC proposing a more compact way to write IPv6 addresses. It is a joke and not a serious proposal.

eli5.summary: A silly idea for squeezing a long address into fewer characters. It was written as a prank on April Fools Day, not for real use.

questions: what is the base 85 ipv6 joke rfc
subtitle: An April Fools joke proposing base-85 encoding for IPv6 addresses

tldr.problem: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, requiring 32 hex digits plus punctuation—up to 39 characters—which is cumbersome to write.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC (published April 1, 1996) proposes treating the address as a single 128-bit integer, encoding it in base 85, and representing it in 20 bytes using a special 85-character set. The character set avoids punctuation that conflicts with common syntax (quotes, slashes, colons, brackets).
tldr.outcome: A mathematically sound but impractical joke; the encoding reduces length but is unreadable and requires 128-bit arithmetic.

today: RFC 1924 is Informational and was never adopted. IPv6 addresses are still written using standard hex notation with optional zero suppression. The base-85 encoding remains a notable example of RFC humor and mathematical cleverness in service of an impractical goal.

sections.title: The Setup
sections.content:
This RFC is an April Fools joke, published on 1 April 1996. It proposes encoding IPv6 addresses using base-85 notation, which would reduce them from up to 39 characters to exactly 20 characters. While the math is correct and the spec is detailed, it is not intended as a serious proposal and was never adopted.

The author's tone is deadpan; the document is phrased as a serious technical specification, building humor through false earnestness.
sections.eli5: This is a funny April Fools joke where someone pretended to solve the problem of long IPv6 addresses by making them into nonsense strings.

sections.title: How the Encoding Works
sections.content:
The scheme treats a 128-bit IPv6 address as a single integer and converts it to base 85. Since 85^20 is large enough to represent all 2^128 possible addresses, exactly 20 characters suffice. Base 85 was chosen as the smallest base that fits in 20 characters (base 84 would need 21; base 94 is the maximum using printable ASCII).

The character set includes digits, letters, and special characters—omitting quotes, commas, periods, slashes, colons, brackets, and backslashes so the address can appear in quotes or CIDR notation. An example address 1080:0:0:0:8:800:200C:417A encodes as 4)+k&C#VzJ4br>0wv%Yp.
sections.eli5: Take the whole IPv6 address as one huge number, convert it to base 85, and you get 20 weird characters. It works mathematically but looks like gibberish.

sections.title: Why This Is a Joke
sections.content:
The RFC treats real problems seriously (IPv6 addresses are long; humans don't learn them) but proposes an absurd solution. The resulting strings are unreadable; the scheme requires 128-bit integer arithmetic, which was not trivial in 1996; and readability is lost entirely. The author notes that the obscurity might even be a security feature—an address in base-85 looks like random gibberish to a packet sniffer.

The joke works because it is technically sound but practically useless, mirroring the earnest-but-absurd tone of some real RFC specifications.
sections.eli5: It's a funny idea because it technically works but nobody could actually use it. Writing addresses as 4)+k&C#VzJ4br>0wv%Yp is worse than writing them the normal way.
